advances: Exact replacement of actual cap normals on the marked plane, with the slack of the new cap accounted for in the original mixed mass. A tie among largest weights and criticality of the new cap are separate hypotheses.

proof:
The displayed dependence is obtained from $\sum_jv_j=0$ by adding the expression for $u/L_0$ and subtracting $\lambda_jv_j/L_0$ for every index. The coefficients of the maximal-weight indices become zero and all other displayed coefficients are strictly positive. The $m-p_0$ retained original normals are independent because they form a proper subset of the sole-dependence family. The relation expresses $u$ in their span. The new family thus has rank $m-p_0$ and its space of dependences is one-dimensional with no zero coefficient, making the dependence minimal. Since the old rank is $m-1$, the rank falls precisely for $p_0\ge2$. Taking dot products with any continuous point proves the closed cover at base zero: the positively weighted sum of the continuous margins is zero, so some margin is nonnegative. The coefficient sum is
$$
1/L_0+(m-p_0)-(1-p_0L_0)/L_0=m.
$$
Every ambient normal has base component $-1$, so the weighted base component is preserved. This continuous balance does not assert coverage of every ambient plane at positive base.

For the mass assertion every retained original label costs $Q$ in the original mixed measure and the one new label costs $Q+\Delta$ with weight $1/L_0$. The coefficient sum gives the claimed accounting. If the separating inequality holds, then the averaged cap takes all of $A$ and has only a null level-one trace on $B$ because $u\ne0$ by independence of the normals excluding $i$. Its original mixed mass is then exactly $|A|+|K\cap\{u\cdot x\ge0\}|$, and it contains $(0,0)$, proving the last assertion.
statement:
Let $d\ge2$, $m=d+1$, and let $v_0,\ldots,v_d$ span $\mathbb R^d$ with the sole dependence generated by $\sum_jv_j=0$. Let $\lambda$ be a probability vector on the indices other than $i$, extended by $\lambda_i=0$, and set $u=\sum_j\lambda_jv_j$, $L_0=\max_j\lambda_j$, and $M_0=\{j:\lambda_j=L_0\}$ with size $p_0$. Replace the normals indexed by $M_0$ by $u$, retaining all other normals. The new minimal positive dependence is
$$
\frac{1}{L_0}u+\sum_{j\notin M_0}(1-\lambda_j/L_0)v_j=0.
$$
The new family has rank $m-p_0$, and the coefficients sum to $m$. Thus the resulting continuous caps through zero cover all of $\mathbb R^d$, with an actual rank reduction exactly when $p_0\ge2$. With ambient normals $(-1,v_j)$ and $(-1,u)$ the displayed weights preserve the total base component $-m$.

In the actual three-fiber model with $A,K,B$ at $-1,0,1$, $B\subseteq T=\{v_j\cdot x\le1\ \forall j\}$, $(A+B)/2\subseteq K$, and $0\in\operatorname{int}K$, suppose the original caps $v_j\cdot x\ge z$ all attain the genuine raw depth $Q$ at $(0,0)$. If the actual averaged cap $u\cdot x\ge z$ has mass $Q+\Delta$, then the weighted total new cap mass equals $mQ+\Delta/L_0$. In particular, if $\min_Au\cdot x\ge-1$, then $\Delta=|A|+|K\cap\{u\cdot x\ge0\}|-Q\ge0$.
title: Averaged-normal replacement has an exact rank and cap cost
